abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a groundbreaking paradigm for computing Gröbner bases through tropical algebraic geometry, fundamentally transforming our approach to polynomial system solving. By establishing a novel connection between tropical semirings and classical Gröbner theory, we develop a preprocessing technique that characterizes the solution structure before engaging in expensive algebraic computation. The tropical perspective enables us to determine critical structural properties of the input ideal, including dimension, degree bounds, and regularity conditions, through computationally efficient combinatorial operations. Our main theoretical contribution proves that the tropical variety computation can be performed in singly exponential time in the number of variables, while the subsequent Gröbner basis computation exhibits dramatically reduced complexity due to the extracted structural information. This two-phase paradigm shifts the computational paradigm from monolithic elimination to hierarchical structure exploitation. Complexity analysis demonstrates exponential improvement in the worst-case bound compared to classical algorithms. Experimental implementation on benchmarks from computer vision and robotics validates the theoretical predictions, showing order-of-magnitude speedups for polynomial systems with underlying geometric structure. This work opens new research directions at the intersection of tropical geometry and computer algebra.

We present substantial improvements to the complexity bounds for solving structured polynomial systems that arise frequently in algebraic cryptanalysis and coding theory. While classical resultants and Gröbner basis algorithms exhibit doubly exponential complexity in the number of variables, many practical instances exhibit much better behavior that is not captured by existing theory. Our analysis introduces the concept of polynomial system rigidity in the context of elimination theory, characterizing input families for which elimination exhibits significantly better complexity. By exploiting the sparsity pattern and algebraic dependence structure inherent in cryptographic and combinatorial polynomial systems, we derive refined complexity bounds of O(n^ω log D) for the computation of resultants, where n denotes the number of variables, ω is the matrix multiplication exponent, and D bounds the degrees. This represents a dramatic improvement over the naive O(D^n) bound. Furthermore, we develop a new incremental elimination algorithm that achieves the refined complexity while providing intermediate computational artifacts useful for subsequent analysis. Applications to algebraic attacks on multivariate cryptosystems and decoding problems for algebraic geometry codes demonstrate that our theoretical improvements translate directly into practical efficiency gains, enabling the solution of previously intractable problem instances.

We present a novel computer algebra system architecture designed from first principles to exploit the characteristics of modern heterogeneous computing platforms. Traditional computer algebra systems emerged in the era of single-core processors and have accumulated decades of design decisions that now impede performance. Our system, tentatively named AlgebrI, abandons these legacy constraints in favor of a modular architecture comprising three novel components: a persistent ideal representation supporting lazy evaluation, a parallel reduction engine utilizing work-stealing schedulers optimized for symbolic manipulation, and a heterogeneous dispatch layer enabling seamless utilization of GPUs and specialized accelerators for specific algebraic operations. The ideal representation employs a canonical form that simultaneously supports efficient membership testing, ideal operations, and geometric queries. Our parallel engine introduces symbolic-aware load balancing strategies that outperform general-purpose schedulers by an order of magnitude for typical computer algebra workloads. The dispatch layer automatically selects optimal algorithms based on input characteristics and hardware topology. Comprehensive benchmarks demonstrate that AlgebrI achieves two to three orders of magnitude speedup over established systems including Singular and Macaulay2 for large-scale polynomial system computations. The system includes a domain-specific language for specifying algebraic algorithms, enabling rapid prototyping of new methods while maintaining production-quality performance.

We describe a comprehensive redesign of quantifier elimination procedures within the CAD framework, achieving substantial practical improvements over state-of-the-art implementations. The core innovation lies in an adaptive algorithm selection mechanism that dynamically chooses among competing elimination strategies based on real-time problem characteristics. Our system integrates cylindrical algebraic decomposition with virtual substitution and partial cylindrical algebraic decomposition, selecting the most promising approach through a learned cost model trained on extensive problem instances. Key algorithmic contributions include an improved projection operator that reduces the number of projection factors by exploiting algebraic independence, an enhanced lifting phase with optimized CAD cell construction, and a caching mechanism that enables effective reuse of computational artifacts across related queries. The implementation incorporates symbolic-numeric computation techniques, enabling graceful degradation when exact arithmetic becomes prohibitively expensive while maintaining correctness guarantees for the quantifier-free formula. Extensive experimental evaluation on standard benchmarks from the SMT-LIB repository demonstrates a factor of 3.7 improvement in average running time compared to the best existing CAD implementation, with more substantial gains on problems exhibiting special structure. The system is fully integrated into an open-source computer algebra platform and supports user-extensible theory solvers.
